v.rationale: I rank impl-1 first, narrowly. Both test suites pass (impl-1: 21 tests, impl-2: 28 tests). The two implementations are nearly identical in structure and Http client use. Both have the same timeout budget, the same retry limited to connection errors and 5xx, a renderable UnknownPostcode for the 404, a try/catch fallback in the controller, and preventStrayRequests plus Sleep::fake in Pest.php. Probes covered a 429 (one attempt then fallback in both), a non-JSON 200 (fallback in both), a trailing newline (accepted in both because TrimStrings strips it) and Arabic-Indic digits (422 in both). The deciding difference is that impl-2 returns 500 when the carrier sends a 200 with a non-array `rates`, because `?? throw` only catches null and the TypeError escapes. impl-1's is_array guard serves the fallback. impl-2 is better on idiom: a dedicated exception for the 401 alert, named constants, an int cast on the fallback, and broader tests. But a reachable 500 on a flaky partner's malformed response breaks the checkout, which this endpoint exists to prevent. That bug outweighs impl-1's weaker 401 alerting and its missing int cast, which only matters when config is overridden at runtime.

That retries quickly during an outage, though the 5/s global limiter bounds it. impl-2's 5 s floor is better there. impl-2 also adds a little ceremony: a WarehouseClient service, an empty exception class and WithoutOverlapping. In exchange it has slightly nicer test techniques for the mail failure and the rendered email.

v.rationale: All three suites pass. All three resolve production config correctly. I probed each in a clean child process with only the six production variables: the host becomes tls://<endpoint>, user is shop, timeouts are 1 s, phpredis retries are 0, the lock connection is `cache`, and value and lock keys start with `shop:`. Each app boots locally on the database store, survives `config:cache`, and passed throwaway probes for env leaks across random test order and for lock owners. Runtime timeout probes were not possible: phpredis is not installed here and local port binding is blocked, so worst-case timings come from reading vendor code. In Laravel 13.44, a lost connection triggers a client rebuild (connect plus AUTH) and one retry. With 1 s timeouts that is about 4 s per call for all three. No implementation stops several calls in one request from adding up past 5 s, and only impl-3 says so. impl-1 ranks first. It has the cleanest config (one shared connection array, no SELECT) and the strongest tests (exact-env child process, checks the resolved lock connection, formatted TLS host and exit code). Its plan pauses workers and the scheduler and empties the tables before rollback. Its flaw is using queue:restart to stop workers. impl-2 ranks second. Its plan is the safest (scale workers to 0) and it guards empty timeout env values. But its tests change process env in-process and grep source files, it keeps SELECT 1 and duplicated blocks, and it undercounts the worst case as 3 s. impl-3 ranks last. Its config is fine, but its cutover rolls workers and the scheduler during the overlap and accepts duplicate unique or overlap jobs. Its rollback leaves stale database cache in place.

v.rationale:
All three take the same core approach. They route the cache and its locks to the `cache` connection, default REDIS_PREFIX to `shop:`, read REDIS_SCHEME so phpredis connects to tls://, set 1 s connect and read timeouts, and turn off phpredis retries. All test suites pass.

Live timeout probes were not possible: phpredis is not installed and the sandbox blocks local port binding. The probes were config-level instead: booting each app with only the production env, with empty timeout vars, with nothing set, and with a polluted .env. I also checked the timeout claims against the installed Laravel 13.44 retry code.

impl-1 ranks first. It has a DRY shared connection array, sends no SELECT, and has tests that really isolate production env from .env and check the formatted host and lock connection. Its cutover plan pauses the scheduler and workers and handles rollback staleness. Its faults are small: inconsistent timeout formulas, a wrong claim about tags, and an empty-env timeout of 0.

impl-2 has the best cutover doc and guards empty timeout values. But it keeps SELECT on database 1, which forces an ACL change on a shared node. It understates the worst-case timeout. Its tests change global env and read the local .env, and they failed when .env was polluted.

impl-3 is clean and well tested. But its rollback brings back stale database cache values, and its single roll lets background work overlap across the two stores instead of pausing it. Both are real problems in the area the task focuses on.

v.rationale: All three use the same core design. A read-through helper treats a Valkey error as a cache miss, reports it, and skips Valkey for the rest of the request (or for a cooldown) after the first failure. That keeps each token check at about one 2 s Valkey timeout plus the 3 s IdP call, and keys always come from the IdP while Valkey is down. All suites pass. Probes covered the real redis store failing (it throws Error 'Class Redis not found' here), write-only failure, lock release failure, a cached false result and lock contention. impl-1 and impl-2 handled all of these. impl-3 exits 0 when another payouts run holds the lock. The task explicitly requires a failure code whenever the lock cannot be taken, and impl-3 kept the old test asserting success. Its resume test also never brings the failing store back, so it proves nothing. impl-3 ranks last despite having the clearest ops signal (the ValkeyUnavailable exception). impl-1 and impl-2 are close. impl-2 edges ahead: it uses the #[Scoped] container attribute, sets max_retries to 0 so reconnect backoff cannot eat the 6 s budget, and has a config test pinning that. Its request-identity tracking is extra ceremony. impl-1's time-based cooldown also works in long-lived processes, and its production-env test is valuable but heavy. impl-1 also leaves retries at 3 and adds unrelated config churn.

v.rationale: All three use the same core design: a wrapper that treats cache errors as misses, reports them, and skips Valkey after the first failure. Each passes its own suite. My probes confirmed one store call and about 0.8 s per request against a slow failing store, correct results when a put fails, and correct handling of a cached false. impl-3 fails a hard requirement: when the lock is held by another run, payouts:run still exits 0. v.rationale:
I ranked impl-2 first, impl-3 second and impl-1 third. All three suites pass (24/24, 12/12 and 11/11). There is no phpredis or Valkey here, so the probes cover config, provisioning, job behaviour and scheme handling, not live Redis connections.

**impl-2 (rank 1):** best on the focus area.
- Explicit connect and read timeouts. A separate queue Redis connection has a read_timeout longer than block_for=2, so no call hangs and BLPOP never times out.
- Empty env values fall back to defaults. Horizon's copied connection prefix is tested to start with shop:.
- Broadest tests, including an end-to-end worker run, gate allow/deny and the no-env fallback.
- One real bug: the '*' environment comes before 'local' and Horizon takes the first match, so local never applies. The env-juggling test helper and the duplicated connection block add ceremony.

**impl-3 (rank 2):** simple and correct.
- Environments are in the right order and block_for is 5.
- It relies on implicit phpredis timeouts and doesn't handle an empty REDIS_SCHEME.
- The job inserts with DB::table and sets timestamps by hand instead of using a model.

**impl-1 (rank 3):** weakest.
- It leaves block_for null, so workers fall back to Horizon's 3s sleep.
- It adds a unique index plus createOrFirst. A probe showed a second reminder for the same invoice is silently dropped, which contradicts "handle() inserts a row".
- Several tests are vacuous, for example asserting app()->isBooted().
- No timeouts are set, and tries/backoff appear in both the job and the Horizon config.
